**Answer (from retrieved chunks only):** The retrieved evidence—all from one paper, `immunology__2604.01385__strategies-for-tumor-elimination-and-control`—identifies several tumor-control strategies. Adaptive therapy seeks to control rather than eliminate the tumor by maintaining a balance between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cells, while combination therapy (e.g., chemotherapy plus immunotherapy targeting different vulnerabilities) reduces the likelihood any single clone survives, though success depends heavily on timing, dosing, and sequence. Combination therapy consistently expands the parameter region corresponding to tumor control and delays resistance emergence. Therapy should be phenotype-guided: when the immune-resistant subpopulation using immune checkpoint regulation dominates, control is highly sensitive to immune exhaustion, so checkpoint inhibitors combined with moderate chemotherapy are most effective (via decreasing immune exhaustion μ or increasing activation ρ, σ); when reduced antigen presentation drives resistance, checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T therapy, or cancer vaccines (increasing effector recruitment ρ, lowering μ) are supported; when the immune-sensitive phenotype dominates, boosting effector recruitment and persistence via adoptive T-cell transfer or cytotoxic therapy is preferred. The model also proposes sequential treatment strategies guided by measurable biological markers, since small parameter changes can shift outcomes between elimination, coexistence, and dominance regimes.
